George Frideric Handel. A German-born Baroque composer who spent most of his career in London, becoming the towering musical figure of eighteenth-century England. Master of both operatic drama and monumental choral works, he composed operas, oratorios, concertos, and orchestral suites of unsurpassed craftsmanship and immediate emotional appeal.

Born in Halle, Germany, Handel trained in Italy before settling in London, where he became the dominant musical force from the seventeen-twenties onward. He composed approximately forty operas in the Italian style, featuring elaborate coloratura roles for castrati singers and heroic narratives from classical antiquity and mythology.

Handel created monumental choral works, particularly oratorios, which became his primary focus after the operatic market declined. The most famous is Messiah, from seventeen forty-two, containing the beloved Hallelujah chorus. He also wrote Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks, two celebrated instrumental suites composed for public court occasions, showcasing brilliant orchestration and popular appeal.

Handel was master of the concerto grosso form, alternating between a small group of soloists and the full orchestra, creating dynamic textural contrast. He received royal patronage from Kings George the First and George the Second, and his music became central to English civic, religious, and courtly life. He maintained a mastery of counterpoint rivaling Bach's, combined with an incomparable gift for immediate, singable melody, making his works accessible yet sophisticated.

His works defined the Baroque aesthetic in England and influenced generations of composers. He is a contemporary and fellow Baroque master alongside Bach, and his concerto forms were influenced by fellow Baroque virtuoso Antonio Vivaldi. Handel spent the majority of his career in England, his adopted home where he created his greatest works, wielding counterpoint as a compositional technique with mastery throughout his career.
